_note: The Gym manifest (WP25a): which grammar points act as selectable form categories, grouped into picker columns. 'point' must match the grammar point title exactly (resolved to ids at request time). 'usage' is the plain-language hover explanation; 'example' is a real drill sentence from that point. 'nonstandard': entries hidden behind the 'include non-standard words' toggle.

entries.point: Subject concords and the present (ndi-, u-, ba-…)
entries.label: Present
entries.usage: Use it for what someone does now or as a rule: the front piece says who (ndi- I, u- you, ba- they), and -ya- goes in only when nothing follows the verb.
entries.example: Ndifunda isiXhosa. — I study Xhosa.

entries.label: Present negative
entries.usage: Use it to say someone does not do something: the verb gains a- at the front and swaps its last vowel to -i, so ndiyafunda becomes andifundi.
entries.example: Andithethi isiNgesi. — I don't speak English.

entries.label: Recent past
entries.usage: Use it for something finished today or lately, when the verb ends the sentence: it closes with -ile.
entries.example: Ndifundile. — I have studied.

entries.label: Remote past
entries.usage: Use it for things that happened long ago and for telling a story: ndi- fuses with -a- into nda-.
entries.example: Ndahlala eKapa kudala. — I lived in Cape Town long ago.

entries.label: Past continuous
entries.usage: Use it for what was going on at some past moment, often when something else interrupted: be- fuses onto the front, bendifunda.
entries.example: Bendifunda incwadi izolo. — I was reading a book yesterday.

entries.label: Future
entries.usage: Use it for anything still to come: -za before the verb with ku- on it, Ndiza kufunda.
entries.example: Ndiza kufunda ngomso. — I will study tomorrow.

entries.label: Negative past/future
entries.usage: Use it to deny something that happened or will happen: a-…-anga for the past (andifundanga) and a-…-zi ku- for the future (andizi kufunda).
entries.example: Andifundanga izolo. — I didn't study yesterday.

entries.label: Subjunctive / let's
entries.usage: Use it to propose doing something together, or to say what you want someone else to do: the verb ends in -e instead of -a.
entries.example: Masifunde! — Let's study!

entries.label: Still / no longer
entries.usage: Use -sa- to say something is still going on (ndisafunda), and its negative to say it has stopped (andisahlali apha).
entries.example: Ndisafunda isiXhosa. — I am still learning Xhosa.

entries.label: May / can
entries.usage: Use -nga- to ask permission or say something is possible: ndingakunceda? — may I help you?
entries.example: 'Ndingakunceda?' wabuza unovenkile. — 'May I help you?' asked the shopkeeper.

entries.label: Object concords
entries.usage: Use it when both of you already know what is being talked about, so it rides inside the verb instead of being named again.
entries.example: Incwadi? Ndiyayifunda. — The book? I am reading it.

entries.label: Passive
entries.usage: Use it when what matters is what was done, not who did it: a -w- slips in before the last vowel, funda becomes fundwa.
entries.example: Incwadi iyafundwa. — The book is being read.

entries.label: Causative
entries.usage: Use -isa when someone makes or gets something done: funda (learn) becomes fundisa (teach), sebenza (work) becomes sebenzisa (use).
entries.example: Utitshala ufundisa abantwana. — The teacher teaches the children.

entries.label: Applicative
entries.usage: Use -ela when the action is done for, to or towards someone: bhala (write) becomes bhalela (write to someone).
entries.example: Ndibhalela umama ileta. — I am writing a letter to mother.

entries.label: Reciprocal
entries.usage: Use -ana when two or more people do it to each other: thanda (love) becomes thandana (love each other).
entries.example: Bayathandana. — They love each other.

entries.label: Stative (-eka)
entries.usage: Use -eka or -akala to say something can be seen, heard or found, without naming anyone who does it — and for the everyday kufuneka, it is necessary.
entries.example: Intaba iyabonakala kude. — The mountain is visible from afar.

entries.label: Have (-na-)
entries.usage: Use -na- to say what someone has; it melts into the noun that follows, so ndi + imali becomes ndinemali.
entries.example: Ndinencwadi entle. — I have a beautiful book.

entries.label: Classes 1/2 (people)
entries.usage: Use these for people: um- for one (umfundi, a student) and aba- for more than one (abafundi).
entries.example: Umfundi omnye, abafundi ababini. — One student, two students.

entries.label: Classes 5/6, 7/8
entries.usage: Use i-/ama- for things like iqanda and amaqanda, and isi-/izi- for isitya and izitya — isi- also names languages, isiXhosa.
entries.example: Iqanda elinye, amaqanda amabini. — One egg, two eggs.

entries.label: Classes 9/10
entries.usage: Use these for most everyday things and for animals: inja becomes izinja, incwadi becomes iincwadi with a long ii-.
entries.example: Inja enye, izinja ezimbini. — One dog, two dogs.

entries.label: Classes 11/14/15
entries.usage: Use ulu- for things like ulwimi (language), ubu- for ideas like ubomi (life), and uku- when a verb is used as a thing, ukutya (food).
entries.example: Ulwimi lwesiXhosa luhle. — The Xhosa language is beautiful.

entries.label: It is (ngu-/yi-)
entries.usage: Use it to say what or who something is: ngu- in front of names and people, yi- in front of class-9 nouns like incwadi.
entries.example: NguThemba lo. — This is Themba.

entries.label: Possessives
entries.usage: Use it to say whose something is: the ending stays put (-m my, -kho your, -khe his/her) while the first letter copies the thing owned, incwadi yam but umntwana wam.
entries.example: Incwadi yam ilahlekile. — My book is lost.

entries.label: Adjectives
entries.usage: Use it whenever you describe a noun: the describing word takes a front piece copied from that noun, umntwana omhle but incwadi entle.
entries.example: umntwana omhle — a beautiful child

entries.label: This / that
entries.usage: Use these to point at something near you (lo mntu, le ncwadi) or further off, where the word lengthens to loo, leyo.
entries.example: Lo mntu uyafunda. — This person is studying.

entries.label: Emphatic pronouns
entries.usage: Use mna, wena, yena when you want to stress or contrast who you mean, since the verb already says who is acting.
entries.example: Mna ndiyasebenza namhlanje. — As for ME, I am working today.

entries.label: Counting
entries.usage: Use it to count things or to ask how many: the number copies the noun it counts, abantu ababini but iincwadi ezimbini.
entries.example: Ndineencwadi ezimbini. — I have two books.

entries.label: Places (e-…-ini)
entries.usage: Use it to say where something is or where you are going: the place word takes e- in front and often -ini on the end, isikolo becomes esikolweni.
entries.example: Ndihlala eKapa. — I live in Cape Town.

entries.label: By / with (nga-)
entries.usage: Use nga- to say how, with what or when something is done: ngemoto (by car), ngesiXhosa (in Xhosa), ngoMvulo (on Monday).
entries.example: Siza kuhamba ngemoto. — We will travel by car.

entries.label: Questions
entries.usage: Use these to ask for information; the question word comes after the verb, and a yes/no question just needs rising intonation or Ingaba in front.
entries.example: Ufuna ntoni? — What do you want?

entries.label: Relative clauses
entries.usage: Use it to pick out which one you mean by what it does: the verb gets a front piece and -yo on the end, umntwana ofundayo.
entries.example: umntwana ofundayo — the child who studies

entries.label: If / that (ukuba)
entries.usage: Use ukuba to set up a condition (if you study, you will pass) and to report what someone knows or says (I know that you are coming).
entries.example: Ukuba uyafunda, uza kuphumelela. — If you study, you will pass.

entries.label: When (xa)
entries.usage: Use xa for when or while something happens; the verb in that half drops -ya- and u- shifts to e-, xa utitshala ethetha.
entries.example: Xa ndifunda, ndimamela umculo. — When I study, I listen to music.

entries.label: So that (ukuze)
entries.usage: Use ukuze to give the point of doing something, with the following verb ending in -e.
entries.example: Funda kakhulu ukuze uphumelele. — Study hard so that you pass.

entries.label: Because & why
entries.usage: Use kuba or ngoba to give a reason, and kutheni … nje to ask for one.
entries.example: Andiyi esikolweni kuba ndiyagula. — I am not going to school because I am ill.

entries.label: Ideophones
entries.usage: Use one to drop a vivid sound or sudden image into a story, carried by the verb -thi: wathi cwaka, it went dead silent.
entries.example: Indlu yathi cwaka. — The house went dead silent.

entries.label: Proverbs
entries.usage: Use a proverb to settle a point the way an elder would; umntu ngumntu ngabantu is the one every speaker knows.
entries.example: Umntu ngumntu ngabantu. — A person is a person through people.

entries.label: Respect register
entries.usage: Use it with elders and in-laws: greet them in the plural (molweni), call them tata or mama rather than by name, and treat them ngembeko.
entries.example: 'Molweni, tata.' watsho umfana ehlonipha. — 'Greetings (respectful plural), father,' said the young man politely.

entries.label: Discourse particles
entries.usage: Drop these small words in to steer a conversation: ke moves it along, nje softens, kaloku appeals to what you both know, andithi asks for agreement.
entries.example: Masihambe ke. — Let's go, then.

entries.label: Greetings
entries.usage: Use these to open and close a conversation: molo to one person, molweni to several or to an elder, hamba kakuhle to whoever is leaving and sala kakuhle to whoever stays.
entries.example: 'Molo!' 'Molo, unjani?' — 'Hello!' 'Hello, how are you?'
